challenges.headline: "Edit" really means supersession

challenges.recommendation: Define the re-approval circuit's composition explicitly with whoever owns document compliance before scoping the build.

challenges.headline: Unscoped reopen rights

challenges.recommendation: Define eligibility and reopen permissions explicitly before the feature is scoped further.

challenges.headline: Original recipients stay unaware
challenges.premise: The request only addresses producing a corrected, re-approved document, not what happens to people or systems that already hold or reference the original signed version.
challenges.alternative: Treat existing holders/references as first-class part of the workflow: notify them on supersession and mark the old version explicitly superseded wherever it is displayed or linked.
challenges.consequence: Without this, people keep acting on a version that is no longer current, and the whole point of re-approval — correctness — is defeated in practice.
challenges.recommendation: Map who/what currently references signed documents before finalizing the workflow design.

briefs.solution: A version-supersession workflow: editing a signed document creates a new version, retains and stamps the old one as superseded, re-opens the approval/signature circuit for the new version, and logs the whole action for audit.

challenges.headline: In-place edit vs. new version
challenges.premise: The request is phrased as 'let managers edit and re-approve documents' as if the signed content itself is being modified.
challenges.alternative: Model this as version supersession: a new version is created, the old one is retained and stamped superseded, and the original signatures stay intact and legally attached to the version they signed — nothing about the past is rewritten.
challenges.consequence: Building this as an in-place mutation of signed content would invalidate the original signatures' legal value and silently break the audit trail the platform is relied on for.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client, before estimating, that supersession (not in-place editing) is the intended mechanism.

challenges.headline: Unscoped re-edit trigger
challenges.premise: The request implies any manager can edit any signed document at any time, with no stated boundaries.
challenges.alternative: Bound the rule explicitly — e.g. only before publication, only within a correction window, or only for specific document types/classifications — rather than a blanket 'any signed document, any time' rule.
challenges.consequence: An unscoped rule is a much larger and riskier build (it touches every document type and classification at once) and is harder to defend at audit time than a narrowly bounded correction path.
challenges.recommendation: Define the exact conditions under which re-editing a signed document is permitted before designing the workflow.

challenges.headline: Full re-signature assumed
challenges.premise: The request assumes 're-approve' means the same approval circuit runs again in full for every edit.
challenges.alternative: A lighter re-approval path (e.g. only the editing manager plus one reviewer) may be appropriate for minor corrections, with the full circuit reserved for substantive changes.
challenges.consequence: Assuming full re-signature by default either overbuilds a heavy flow for small corrections or, if wrongly relaxed, quietly weakens the segregation-of-duties the original approval was meant to enforce.
challenges.recommendation: Clarify with stakeholders whether re-approval should mirror the original circuit or a reduced one, and whether that choice should vary by document type.

decisions.decision: An audit trail capturing the prior version, the new version, who edited, who re-approved, and when is a mandatory part of this build.
The objects in scope are Document, Version, Approval and Signatory, per the platform's standard model.

exclusions.option: Building a fully configurable, per-client/per-document-type re-approval engine in this phase
exclusions.reason: The scope of when and for whom this is even allowed is still undefined; configuring an engine before the rule itself is scoped risks building the wrong thing.

exclusions.option: Full reconciliation logic for every downstream system that might reference a signed version
exclusions.reason: No downstream dependency has been confirmed yet — building reconciliation for unconfirmed integrations would be speculative scope expansion.

thresholds.condition: Edits to signed documents turn out to be a frequent, recurring need rather than a rare correction
thresholds.measure: how often managers actually need to re-edit and re-approve a signed document once in production
thresholds.action: invest in a dedicated lighter/faster re-approval path instead of always re-running the full original circuit

thresholds.condition: Different document types or classifications need different re-approval rules
thresholds.measure: whether the same edit-then-reapprove rule applies uniformly or varies by document type/classification
thresholds.action: move the business rule from a fixed default into a per-client/document-type configuration

open_decisions: Version supersession vs. in-place edit for signed documents
Full re-signature by all original approvers vs. a lighter re-approval path
Which document types/classifications and conditions this applies to
The actual driver behind the request (error correction vs. recurring policy update) and its frequency
How readers/downstream consumers are notified and which version is treated as current while re-approval is pending
Whether any downstream system references the specific signed version and needs reconciliation after supersession
